paper.title: Sectoral green finance thresholds for managing carbon transition risks: an input–output network approach with evidence from Malaysia
paper.abstract: Abstract Green finance is an important instrument for supporting low-carbon transitions; however, its effectiveness depends on targeted allocation that balances emission reduction with economic stability. In Malaysia, which has committed to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050, the sectoral distribution of green finance remains uncertain, particularly given complex inter-industry linkages. This study addresses this issue by developing a sectoral input–output framework to estimate indicative green finance thresholds associated with managing carbon transition risks. The approach integrates carbon intensity (CI) and Hypothetical Extraction Centrality (HEC) to capture environmental exposure and systemic importance across the national production network. The results suggest that implied green finance needs are concentrated in a limited number of sectors. Electrical and optical equipment emerges as a systemically important sector, while electricity, gas, and water supply show high carbon intensity. Additional sectors, including coke, refined petroleum and nuclear fuel, wholesale and retail trade, and basic and fabricated metals, are associated with relatively higher estimated financing levels. In contrast, service-oriented sectors appear to exhibit lower transition risks. Overall, the findings highlight how scenario-based, sector-specific allocation can provide insights into potential pathways for reducing emissions while maintaining macroeconomic stability. However, these estimates are best understood as indicative, model-based benchmarks that reflect the structural assumptions of a static, one-period input–output framework. The study offers a scalable analytical approach that may help inform green finance discussions in Malaysia and other emerging economies.

review.reason: The paper develops an input–output framework to estimate sectoral green finance thresholds for carbon transition risk management, which is a finance/ESG allocation application rather than environmental accounting of physical capital formation, capital stocks, or infrastructure, and it does not couple a transferable prospective IO/MRIO method to IAM/SSP future scenarios.
review.methodology: Static one-period input–output framework integrating carbon intensity and Hypothetical Extraction Centrality
review.research_object: Sectoral green finance thresholds and carbon transition risks in Malaysia
review.environmental_dimension: Carbon intensity and emissions exposure across sectors

paper.title: Environmental and socio-economic implications of solar photovoltaic reshoring under the EU Net Zero Industry Act: a hybrid input–output assessment
paper.abstract: Abstract The photovoltaic supply chain is complex and geographically concentrated. Assessing the impacts of policies targeting it requires models that explicitly represent supply-chain structure. While process-based life-cycle assessment truncates economy-wide effects and top-down input–output models are too aggregated to resolve individual manufacturing stages, our study develops a hybrid framework integrating a process-based PV supply chain model into the multi-regional input–output accounting structure of EXIOBASE. The model is first verified against reference literature ranges of solar electricity carbon footprints and producer prices, showing literature-consistent results that purely top-down models miss by omitting productive capital. The framework is applied to the Net Zero Industry Act, a major European Union (EU) reshoring policy, under a scenario where 40% of module demand is supplied domestically. Results show that reshoring mainly affects downstream stages, while upstream production remains largely external, leading to moderate changes in consumption-based emissions and limited gains in EU value-added and employment.

review.reason: The paper develops a hybrid process-based PV supply-chain model integrated into EXIOBASE MRIO to assess environmental and socio-economic impacts of EU solar reshoring, explicitly accounting for productive capital and consumption-based emissions.
review.methodology: Hybrid process-based life-cycle model integrated into EXIOBASE multi-regional input-output accounting, applied to a Net Zero Industry Act reshoring scenario
review.research_object: Solar photovoltaic supply chain and EU reshoring policy (Net Zero Industry Act)
review.environmental_dimension: Consumption-based emissions and carbon footprints of solar electricity

paper.title: Wood use scenarios in Sweden through integrated monetary-physical input–output framework
authors: de la Maza Larrea, Arrate Sainz
paper.abstract: Abstract Governments promote expanded wood use to meet climate and bioeconomy goals, yet policy requires comprehensive evidence. We develop an integrated monetary-physical input–output framework for Sweden linking structural changes in wood use to macroeconomic performance, GHG emissions, and carbon stock dynamics in wood-based products and forests. We simulate 3 stylised scenarios for 2020–2040: (i) cross-laminated timber (CLT) construction; (ii) waste recycling; and (iii) wood cascade combining both with a harvest constraint met by reduced pulp and paper demand. Across scenarios, aggregate economic and production-based GHG effects remain modest at the national level, while impacts on the forest-based economy and carbon-stock trajectories are more pronounced. CLT construction delivers the strongest macroeconomic gains (value added +5.1 bn SEK yr⁻ 1 ; employment +8.5 thousand yr⁻ 1 ) and lowers production-based GHG emissions (− 0.3 Mt CO₂e yr⁻ 1 ), but reduces the forest carbon pool, yielding a negative system carbon balance (− 63 Mt carbon (C) by 2040). Waste recycling increases value added (+ 4.3 bn SEK yr⁻ 1 ) and improves system carbon (+ 7 Mt C by 2040). Wood cascade increases value added (+ 2.4 bn SEK yr⁻ 1 ), achieves the largest GHG reduction (− 0.53 Mt CO₂e yr⁻ 1 ), and yields a positive system carbon trajectory (+ 33 Mt C by 2040). Overall, cascading secures climate benefits while maintaining economic performance, albeit with a shift away from pulp, paper, and mineral production toward long-lived wood products, whereas substitution without harvest limits risks eroding forest resources and the carbon sink. The framework enables system-wide comparison of wood-use strategies, revealing economy-forest trade-offs and supporting integrated assessment across monetary and physical accounts.

review.reason: The paper develops an integrated monetary-physical input–output framework simulating wood-use scenarios (CLT construction, recycling, cascade) linked to GHG emissions and carbon stock dynamics, directly addressing environmental accounting of capital formation and infrastructure (CLT construction) and prospective IO scenario methods.
review.methodology: Integrated monetary-physical input–output framework with stylised 2020–2040 scenarios
review.research_object: Wood use strategies in Sweden (CLT construction, waste recycling, wood cascade) and their macroeconomic, GHG, and carbon stock effects
review.environmental_dimension: GHG emissions, forest carbon pool and system carbon balance, carbon stock dynamics in wood products

How Long Do Buildings Live: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Global Building Lifetimes
paper.abstract: Abstract Building lifetime is a foundational parameter for modeling stock dynamics, informing environmental impact assessment and urban development, yet current lifetime assumptions frequently lack empirical grounding. Although well-established in medicine and demography, survival analysis concepts have not penetrated building stock research to the same extent. This study bridges this gap through a systematic review and meta-analysis of 258 median building lifetime estimates across 46 global studies. Central to our analysis is right-censoring, when a building’s demolition remains unobserved at the end of the observation period, which, if unaccounted for in estimation, leads to underestimated lifetimes. We systematize five estimation approaches based on data type and the capacity to account for right-censoring, describe the currently available empirical evidence, and apply a meta-regression to identify significant predictors of median lifetimes: world region, use class, structural material, and right-censoring bias, the latter underestimating building lifetimes by 50% (95% CI: 49–51%). Of the five estimation approaches identified, three inherently consider right-censoring, one inherently cannot correct for it, and one requires an active correction step that is frequently omitted. Our work identifies critical data gaps and offers targeted recommendations for users and producers of lifetime estimates to improve transparency, reproducibility, and methodological rigor.

review.reason: The paper provides empirically grounded building lifetime estimates that are foundational parameters for modeling building stock dynamics and environmental impact assessment, directly supporting capital stock and material stock accounting.
review.methodology: Systematic review and meta-analysis with meta-regression of 258 median building lifetime estimates across 46 studies, including survival analysis and right-censoring correction.
review.research_object: Building lifetimes (median demolition/survival estimates) for building stocks globally.
review.environmental_dimension: Environmental impact assessment via building stock dynamics and material stock modeling.

paper.title: Decomposing Vehicle Production and Consumption Impacts in Japan under Mobility and Production Network Interventions
paper.abstract: Abstract Passenger vehicles contribute approximately 8% to global energy-related emissions and drive other environmental impacts through the extraction of raw materials. In this study, a hybrid LCA approach is used to investigate emissions and material life-cycle impacts arising from vehicle production and consumption in Japan. By embedding a physical vehicle production model within a global MRIO, we find that 53% of emissions occur in Japan, while almost all material extraction impacts occur internationally. Vehicle size, PHEV utility factor, and battery capacity all strongly influence life-cycle impacts. Demand-side scenarios of increased occupancy, downsizing, and lifetime extension have the collective potential to reduce emissions by approximately 33% at the cohort level, while providing comparable mobility services. Lifetime extension requires additional material inputs with associated impacts; however, these impacts are repaid over time, resulting in an overall average emissions intensity (gCO2e/km) reduction of 7%. Vehicle electrification alone is unlikely to be sufficient to meet climate targets; therefore, demand-side measures should be implemented concurrently to decarbonize passenger transport while maintaining access to mobility services. While some opportunity exists to substitute upstream suppliers for lower-impact providers, the existence of low-pollution production havens is limited, further underscoring the importance of demand-side measures.

review.reason: The paper uses a hybrid LCA embedding a physical vehicle production model within a global MRIO to quantify life-cycle emissions and material impacts of vehicle production and consumption, directly addressing environmental accounting of physical capital/investment goods (vehicles).
review.methodology: Hybrid LCA with physical vehicle production model embedded in global MRIO, plus demand-side scenarios
review.research_object: Passenger vehicle production and consumption in Japan
review.environmental_dimension: Life-cycle GHG emissions and material extraction impacts

paper.title: Multi-Scale Multi-Indicator Assessment of Material Recovery Pathways: The Case of the United States Flat Glass Sector
paper.abstract: Abstract Material recovery and circularity analysis offers critical insights for understanding future scenarios and informing strategic decisions toward resource use. However, existing approaches often lack the granularity and breadth needed to capture supply chain dynamics and economy-wide impacts simultaneously. We introduce a novel quantitative framework─Supply Chain Operations Research through Physical Input-Output (SCORPIO)─that addresses this gap by enabling multi-scale assessment of material recovery strategies across both supply chain and macroeconomic levels. To demonstrate SCORPIO’s capabilities, we apply it to flat glass flows in the United States, examining waste valorization practices, including open- and closed-loop recycling. By assessing economic, workforce, and environmental indicators, SCORPIO reveals the potential outcomes and trade-offs of different waste valorization solutions in a holistic manner. Results show that both open-loop and closed-loop recycling of glass from utility solar and commercial buildings have the potential for positive economic impacts at the supply chain and economy level. However, the effect on environmental impacts was less certain, with open-loop recycling generally performing better than closed-loop pathways. This case study illustrates how the SCORPIO framework can support stakeholders navigating the transition toward increased material recovery, offering a methodological foundation applicable to other material systems facing environmental and resource challenges.

review.reason: The paper develops a physical input-output framework (SCORPIO) for multi-scale assessment of material recovery pathways, evaluating environmental, economic, and workforce indicators for flat glass recycling, which constitutes environmental accounting of material recovery and circularity with economy-wide IO methods.
review.methodology: Physical input-output (SCORPIO) framework combined with supply chain operations research for multi-scale material flow and indicator assessment
review.research_object: United States flat glass sector material recovery and waste valorization pathways (open- and closed-loop recycling)
review.environmental_dimension: Environmental impacts and resource use across recycling scenarios, alongside economic and workforce indicators

paper.title: Enabling molecular signaling with temperature and ionic-strength independence or programmable dependence
paper.abstract: Abstract The equilibrium constants of chemical reactions fundamentally depend on temperature, posing challenges for living systems. However, many conformer organisms do not maintain a stable internal temperature. This raises the question: can molecular signaling pathways inherently resist temperature susceptibility? Molecular commutation is a recently discovered, fundamentally distinct mechanism of biological information processing and storage within reversible association/dissociation reactions. Here, we show that molecular commutation enables complex signaling systems that are independent of temperature and ionic strength and, even more generally, programmably dependent on these parameters. Using examples of various DNA logic gates, receptor-activator networks, and systems with complex input–output relationships (e.g., computed as algebraic functions), we demonstrate computationally that introducing compensatory reactions in these networks can render their signaling independent of temperature and ionic strength. We experimentally validate such independence for a case of a YES-logic gate. Finally, we computationally demonstrate networks with outputs that follow predefined functional forms of temperature and ionic strength (e.g., sin(T), where T is temperature). The presented intrinsic capabilities of affinity-based networks provide a remarkable homeostasis and signaling control mechanism that may be used by biological systems of arbitrarily high complexity.

review.reason: The paper studies molecular commutation and DNA logic gates for temperature/ionic-strength-independent signaling, with no environmental accounting of capital formation, investment goods, infrastructure, or transferable IAM–MRIO scenario methods.
review.methodology: Computational modeling and experimental validation of DNA logic gates and receptor-activator networks
review.research_object: Molecular signaling networks and DNA logic gates

paper.title: Characterising the Swiss window stock and retrofit potential using machine-learning
paper.abstract: Abstract Windows strongly influence both operational energy demand and embodied emissions in the construction sector, yet they remain insufficiently represented in national building material stock models. Accurate representation of window materials, energy performance, and renovation state is essential for assessing both operational and embodied climate impacts, and for informing future refurbishment and re-use strategies. This study combines detailed information from energy performance certificates with machine-learning classification. Window frame materials, glazing types, renovation states, and window to wall ratios are derived from energy certificate data for more than 40,000 buildings. Results show an increasing share of plastic frames since the 1990s and increasing window to wall ratio until 2010. We then train supervised machine-learning classifiers on these 40,000 buildings to predict glazing type and frame material for all 1.51 million Swiss residential buildings from building age, size, and location. While double glazing can be identified with a precision of 0.8 and triple glazing with an F1-score of 0.67, frame-material prediction performs lower due to overlapping characteristics between material classes. We preserve stochastic uncertainty when applying the trained classifiers using probabilistic classification and Monte Carlo analysis. The resulting estimates describe the window stock at an aggregate, probabilistic level. We use this stock estimate to assess the retrofit potential of the Swiss window stock to showcase the application of our framework. Double glazing dominates the residential building stock in all cantons (56.2–67.7%). By contrast, potential annual net $$\hbox {CO}_2$$ CO 2 savings per $$\hbox {m}^{2}$$ m 2 window area for a double-to-triple glazing retrofit show three-fold differences across cantons.

review.reason: The paper characterizes the Swiss window material stock and retrofit potential, quantifying embodied/operational climate impacts and CO2 savings, which constitutes environmental accounting of physical capital stock (building components).
review.methodology: Machine-learning classification combined with Monte Carlo probabilistic analysis applied to energy performance certificate data to estimate material stock and retrofit potential.
review.research_object: Swiss residential window stock (frame materials, glazing types, renovation states, window-to-wall ratios) across 1.51 million buildings.
review.environmental_dimension: Embodied emissions and operational energy/CO2 savings from glazing retrofits.

paper.title: Electricity retail pricing as incentives for load optimization in Vietnam
paper.abstract: Abstract Vietnam’s pathway to net-zero emissions by 2050 has so far relied primarily on large-scale renewable energy investments, with limited use of demand-side management. This study evaluates how alternative retail electricity pricing schemes - flat tariffs, Time-of-Use (TOU), Critical Peak Pricing (CPP), and a TOU-CPP hybrid - shape demand flexibility, system costs, emissions, consumer welfare, and reliability in Vietnam. The analysis uses SWITCH 2.0, an integrated capacity expansion and dispatch model with an iterative demand-response module, to Vietnam’s electricity system in 2050.&#xD;&#xD;Relative to flat pricing, the modeled TOU designs reduce total system costs by up to 15% and CO2 emissions by 17.2-37.5%, while increasing consumer welfare. Consecutive TOU blocks capture substantial benefits, whereas adding CPP produces little additional improvement. Endogenous block assignment achieves the lowest system cost and reduces storage investment, but does not yield the lowest emissions or highest consumer welfare. Sensitivity analysis confirms lower unit costs and emissions and higher consumer welfare under consecutive TOU than under matched flat-pricing cases across seven demand-response parameter combinations. However, the magnitude of these benefits depends strongly on the share of load available for within-day rescheduling. Demand shifting toward solar-rich hours also changes transmission utilization, relieving pressure on some corridors while increasing it elsewhere.&#xD;&#xD;The findings support a staged transition toward TOU pricing with simple consecutive blocks, accompanied by enabling technologies and coordinated transmission planning. The results represent conditional system-level outcomes rather than estimates of realized consumer responses or distributional effects.

review.reason: The paper evaluates retail electricity pricing schemes (TOU, CPP) for demand flexibility and emissions using a capacity expansion/dispatch model, which is operational energy and demand-response analysis without substantive physical capital formation, investment goods, capital stock, or transferable IAM-MRIO/IO scenario methods.
review.methodology: SWITCH 2.0 integrated capacity expansion and dispatch model with iterative demand-response module
review.research_object: Vietnam electricity system retail pricing and demand flexibility in 2050

paper.title: Biodiversity credits hold promise, yet credit-generating protocols require safeguards to realize potential
paper.abstract: Abstract Given the existing gap in biodiversity funding, mobilizing private finance will be essential to achieving global biodiversity conservation goals, especially across lower- and middle-income countries with limited capacity and public finance. The emerging voluntary biodiversity market (VBM) holds promise to leverage private finance for biodiversity, but credit-generating protocols must be robust to prevent greenwashing and maximize effectiveness. In this study, the first to move beyond theoretical critiques and general market assessments of the VBM, we extracted details of program structure and crediting issuance from protocols for 13 relatively well-established biodiversity-crediting organizations. With these data, we evaluated protocols’ alignment with both conservation and restoration biology principles and lessons learned from the voluntary carbon market (VCM). We find that action must be taken to improve quantification of biodiversity impacts, especially incorporating patch size and connectivity in crediting and assessing projects on ecologically relevant timelines. Further, safeguards for additionality, leakage, risk, and verification from the VCM must be more robustly integrated in the VBM, and deep engagement and investment in local communities must be improved to ensure durable biodiversity-positive outcomes.

review.reason: The paper evaluates biodiversity-crediting protocols and market safeguards, which is finance/conservation policy rather than environmental accounting of physical capital formation or transferable IAM-MRIO scenario methods.
review.methodology: Protocol content extraction and evaluation against conservation/restoration principles and VCM lessons

paper.title: Constructing Prospective Multiregional Input-Output Tables via Scenario-Constrained Optimization for Future Environmental Footprint Assessment
paper.abstract: Abstract Prospective multiregional input-output (MRIO) tables that integrate scenarios from integrated assessment models (IAMs) support forward-looking environmental footprint analysis, but the trade-off between historical structural fidelity and scenario compliance has not been quantified. We constructed 12 prospective MRIO tables from EXIOBASE 2019 and the IMAGE SSP2 scenario for 2035, including a Leontief-based projection and 11 optimization-based projections under different combinations of scenario constraints on GDP, value added, sector outputs, as well as energy and agriculture consumption. Among the constraints, those on energy and agriculture consumption were satisfied at the highest cost in coefficient deviations from the Leontief-based projection and shifted the corresponding transaction flows most significantly. Regional shares of the global carbon footprint remained stable, but sectoral attribution within each region was substantially reshuffled, and the identification of high-growth consumption hotspots was sensitive to scenario compliance level. Some hotspots persisted at all levels of compliance. The consumption-based carbon footprint driven by China’s final energy demand grew the fastest and emerged as a major new hotspot in 2035. The footprint of livestock consumption showed persistent high growth in multiple regions and India and the Rest of Asia rose in environmental significance through their industrial sectors.

review.reason: The paper constructs prospective MRIO tables by coupling IAM SSP2 scenarios with EXIOBASE via scenario-constrained optimization for future environmental footprint assessment, directly matching Route B.
review.methodology: Scenario-constrained optimization to construct prospective MRIO tables from EXIOBASE 2019 and IMAGE SSP2, with Leontief-based and optimization-based projections
review.research_object: Prospective multiregional input-output tables and consumption-based carbon footprints for 2035
review.environmental_dimension: Consumption-based carbon footprint and environmental significance of sectors/regions

paper.title: Wastewater Treatment Plants as Anchor Infrastructure for Geothermal Energy in Cold Regions
paper.abstract: Abstract Thermal constraints in cold regions suppress biological treatment, increase energy demand, and elevate greenhouse gas emissions of existing wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), and remain a major barrier to the deployment of adequate sanitation infrastructure in many cold-region communities. Where geothermal resources exist, low-enthalpy hydrothermal heat is well matched to this energy gap. Yet, WWTPs are underrecognized anchors for broader geothermal deployment, providing a continuous, weather-independent thermal offtake through which subsurface CAPEX can be amortized. We reframe geothermal-WWTP integration as a system-level enabler that benefits both parts. Using three cascaded configurations for a full-scale WWTP, a rapid techno-economic analysis identifies three trends: energy and carbon savings/revenues alone are insufficient under realistic policy stacks, whereas crediting the upgrade-deferral value of geothermally enhanced treatment makes the project economically favorable across most policy scenarios. Globally, this triple intersection encompasses ∼11,600 catalogued WWTPs serving ∼280 million people, with a further estimate of ∼48 million people in the same regions beyond current service radii. The opportunity is greatest in cold, remote, and underserved communities, where local geothermal resources, treatment intensification, and community-scale demand together carry a case that no single driver could sustain alone.

review.reason: The paper conducts a techno-economic and carbon analysis of integrating geothermal heat with wastewater treatment plant infrastructure, assessing energy and carbon savings and capital amortization of physical infrastructure upgrades.
review.methodology: Rapid techno-economic analysis with three cascaded geothermal-WWTP configurations and policy scenario assessment
review.research_object: Wastewater treatment plants as anchor infrastructure for geothermal energy deployment in cold regions
review.environmental_dimension: Energy and carbon savings, greenhouse gas emissions reduction, and infrastructure capital accounting

paper.title: Toward Ternary Computing Enabled by Origami-Inspired Modular Architectures
paper.abstract: Abstract Modern mechanical computing, being envisioned as a pathway toward structure- and material-level processing, holds potential for intelligent metamaterials and robotics in extreme environments. However, current computing architectures remain constrained by binary paradigms. Here, we introduce an origami-inspired modular architecture that encodes logical mappings into its inherent kinematic responses under an input-output decoupled paradigm, enabling both binary and ternary mechanical computing. Within this emerging paradigm, the multi-stable states of two Kresling origami configurations serve as physical carriers for generating discrete signals, while torsional transitions among these states ensure signal switching, supporting operations from logic gates to advanced arithmetic. Based on this mechanical architecture, we systematically demonstrate seven common logic gates and modular arithmetic half- and full-adders in both binary and ternary systems, revealing challenges and opportunities in advancing multi-valued logic through comparative analysis. The physical platform, along with its accompanying response-programming strategy, represents a simplified and generalized paradigm that supports migration to higher-level mechanical computing mechanisms.

review.reason: The paper develops origami-inspired mechanical computing architectures for binary and ternary logic, with no environmental accounting, capital formation, or input-output/MRIO scenario methods.
